scenes.narration: This chapter is about turning a described workload into a compute decision in seconds, not guessing by vibe. On the associate exam alone, two domains lean directly on what you're about to learn — Designing High Performing Architectures at twenty four percent, and Designing Cost Optimized Architectures at twenty percent — together, forty four percent of the exam. And here's the one number that resolves more of those questions than anything else: A W S Lambda's maximum timeout is nine hundred seconds, fifteen minutes, full stop, with no configuration that raises it.

Three instincts show up over and over in practice-exam mistakes, and every one of them feels reasonable in the moment. First: faced with a performance-sounding question, just reach for the biggest, most expensive instance on the list. Second: any mention of reducing operational overhead triggers an automatic pick of Lambda, regardless of what the workload actually does once it's running. Third: Reserved Instances feel like the disciplined, safe default for anything labeled production, while Spot feels reckless. All three swap out reading the workload's actual shape for a vague feeling of safety — and the exam is built specifically to punish that.

props.heading: "Bigger, newer, or safer-sounding"
bullets: Bigger instance = safer answer — pile on vCPUs and memory whenever a scenario sounds performance-heavy.
Serverless is the modern default — any mention of "less operational overhead" triggers an automatic Lambda pick.
Reserved Instances feel like the responsible choice for anything in production, and Spot feels reckless.

scenes.narration: Each of those instincts collides with something specific and countable. Scaling up the wrong instance family just buys a bigger version of the wrong shape — a memory-hungry cache on a compute-optimized box still starves, no matter how large you go. Defaulting to Lambda runs straight into a wall: nine hundred seconds, fifteen minutes, is the hard maximum for a single invocation, with no setting that raises it, and its execution environment isn't built to hold state between calls either. And treating Reserved Instances as the safe choice ignores that they're a one- or three-year commitment — exactly wrong for a workload that hasn't found its steady state yet. Spot, meanwhile, is usually dramatically cheaper than On-Demand, but only because A W S can reclaim that capacity with a real two-minute warning — fine for a lot of workloads, fatal for the ones that can't tolerate a sudden pause.

props.heading: Real ceilings, not vague best practices
bullets: "Bigger instance" ignores family, not size — a compute-heavy C-family box run bigger just wastes more RAM it never touches.
"Default to Lambda" hits a wall at 900 seconds — a 15-minute hard timeout with no override, and no fix for state that needs to persist across calls.
"Reserved Instances are always safe" ignores commitment risk — Spot is only risky for workloads that can't absorb its real 2-minute interruption notice.

scenes.narration: The letter in an instance type isn't trivia to memorize, it's a signal about which resource A W S over-provisioned on that box. M is general purpose, a balanced ratio with no built-in bottleneck. C is compute-optimized — more vCPU per unit of memory, built for CPU-bound work like video encoding or ad serving. R flips that ratio toward memory, for in-memory caches and datasets that live entirely in RAM. I and D are the storage letters — I for fast local solid-state I O, D for dense, sequential-throughput hard-disk storage. T is burstable, a low baseline that can spend saved-up credits on short spikes, perfect for something that's idle most of the time. And G or P means an attached accelerator — GPU work like machine-learning training or rendering. The trap: a bigger C-family instance is still a compute-heavy ratio. If the bottleneck is memory, no amount of scaling within the same letter fixes it.

rows.label: R — memory optimized
cells: In-memory caches, big datasets in RAM

rows.label: I / D — storage optimized
cells: High random I/O, or large sequential throughput

rows.label: T — burstable
cells: Idle most of the time, occasional spikes

scenes.narration: Placement groups control physical adjacency, and each of the three strategies trades something different for it. Cluster placement groups pack every instance as close together as possible, but only within a single Availability Zone — that confinement is what buys the low-latency, high-throughput adjacency in the first place. Spread placement groups do the opposite: they insist each instance sits on genuinely distinct underlying hardware, which is why they cap out at a small number of running instances per Availability Zone per group. Partition placement groups sit in between — they divide instances into a bounded number of logical partitions, each on separate hardware, which fits workloads like distributed databases that already replicate data across partitions themselves. The exam trap: asking for cluster-level latency and multi-A-Z resilience in the same breath. One placement group can't give you both.

props.heading: Three placement group strategies
steps: Cluster — pack instances tight in one Availability Zone for the lowest latency and highest throughput between them
Spread — put each instance on genuinely distinct hardware, capped at a small number per Availability Zone per group
Partition — divide instances into logical partitions on distinct hardware, matching workloads that already replicate data themselves

scenes.narration: Purchasing option is a second, independent decision layered on top of whichever service you picked. On-Demand carries no commitment and costs the most per hour of the three — that premium is what buys you the freedom to stop whenever you want, which is exactly right for something new or still finding its steady state. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans ask for a one- or three-year commitment in exchange for a real discount deeper than On-Demand — a great trade once you're confident about a workload's size, and a bad one if you're not. Spot has no commitment either, and it's typically the cheapest of the three by a wide margin, but only because A W S can reclaim that capacity with a genuine two-minute warning. Ask one question to pick correctly: can this workload absorb a sudden, short pause? If yes, Spot is usually the right default. If no, and the size is predictable, reach for Reserved Instances or a Savings Plan. If neither, On-Demand is the correct — not the lazy — answer.

props.kicker: THREE BETS ON THE SAME UNCERTAINTY
props.heading: On-Demand vs Reserved/Savings Plans vs Spot

cells: New or unpredictable workloads — you're paying for flexibility
Steady, predictable workloads you're confident about

scenes.narration: Every E C 2 versus Lambda versus Fargate versus Batch question resolves through the same four facts, asked in the same order: how long does one execution run, does it need to hold state across calls, does it need root or OS-level access, and is it queue-driven with a flexible start time. E C 2 is unbounded in duration and gives you full control of the host — the right answer whenever a scenario needs OS-level access or genuinely persistent state. Lambda's ceiling is nine hundred seconds, fifteen minutes, and its execution environment is meant to be stateless — perfect for short, event-driven work, wrong the moment either fact doesn't hold. Fargate removes fleet management entirely for containers with no fifteen-minute ceiling, but still gives you no access to the underlying host. And Batch is an orchestration layer on top of E C 2 or Fargate, built for queue-driven jobs with flexible timing — exactly the shape that can lean on Spot for its discount.

props.heading: EC2 vs Lambda vs Fargate vs Batch

rows.label: AWS Lambda
cells: Meant to be stateless, no OS access
Short, bursty, event- or HTTP-shaped work

rows.label: ECS on Fargate
cells: Best for stateless containers, no OS access

rows.label: AWS Batch
cells: Flexible-timing queued jobs, often on Spot

scenes.narration: Four scripts map to the four mechanisms this chapter actually tests. A cluster placement group script that creates the group and launches every instance in one request, since adding instances later can fail on capacity. A one-off Spot request built on the same run-instances call, just with a market-type flag added. A mixed-instances Auto Scaling group that blends an On-Demand base with a Spot pool in a single group. And a Batch job submission that hands a flexible-timing, queue-driven job to its own scheduler. You're never asked to type these from memory — you're asked to recognize which mechanism a CLI fragment implements.

props.heading: compute-fleet/
lines: │   └── create-cluster-pg.sh      # single-AZ cluster group, launch all at once
│   └── request-spot-instance.sh  # one-off Spot request via run-instances
│   └── mixed-instances-asg.sh    # On-Demand base + Spot pool, one ASG
└── submit-transcode-job.sh   # queue a flexible-timing job onto Batch

scenes.narration: First, create the placement group with strategy set to cluster — that's what asks for the tightest physical adjacency A W S can offer within one Availability Zone. Then launch every instance for that tightly-coupled job in one single run-instances call, all eight at once, into that group — adding instances one at a time later can fail on capacity even when the zone has room elsewhere. For a completely different, interruption-tolerant workload, that same run-instances call can carry a market-type flag marking it as Spot instead. And the flag that actually implements a blended fleet is mixed-instances-policy on an Auto Scaling group — one group, an On-Demand base that survives a Spot interruption wave, and a Spot pool picked by an allocation strategy for the pools statistically least likely to be reclaimed soon.

props.heading: Placement group, then a blended fleet

output: Base On-Demand capacity + Spot pool, allocation strategy: capacity-optimized

scenes.narration: Run this one through the framework by hand. Jobs run anywhere from twenty minutes to four hours — that alone rules out Lambda before anything else, since it blows straight past the fifteen-minute ceiling. The jobs are queue-driven, can start any time overnight, and are explicitly checkpoint-restartable — that flexible timing and queue shape is a textbook fit for A W S Batch, not a bare E C 2 fleet. And because interruption tolerance is stated outright, Batch's compute environment can lean on E C 2-backed Spot capacity for the deep discount the finance stakeholder is asking about — the checkpoint tolerance is precisely what makes that discount safe to take instead of reckless.

profile.name: Meridian Labs
profile.role: Video ingestion pipeline · jobs 20 min–4 hrs · overnight, flexible start · checkpoint-restartable
profile.detail: Meridian ingests raw video uploads all day and needs to transcode them into several output formats overnight. Jobs can start any time in the overnight window and can safely resume from their last checkpoint if interrupted. Cost is the dominant concern, and a finance stakeholder has specifically asked about Spot.
profile.verdict: AWS Batch with an EC2-backed compute environment on Spot — duration alone rules out Lambda, the queue-driven flexible timing points at Batch, and the explicit checkpoint tolerance is what makes Spot's discount safe to take.

scenes.narration: Try these yourself before the answers. First: a scenario says a single job execution reliably takes twenty-two minutes — which compute service does that fact alone eliminate? Second: a workload runs continuously at a stable size that hasn't changed in over a year — which purchasing option captures the deepest reasonable discount without meaningful risk?

questions.prompt: A scenario states that a single job execution reliably takes twenty-two minutes. Which compute service does this fact alone eliminate?
A workload runs continuously at a stable size that hasn't changed in over a year. Which purchasing option captures the deepest reasonable discount without meaningful risk?
options: On-Demand, because flexibility is always worth paying for
Spot, because it's typically the cheapest option available
Reserved Instances or a Savings Plan, because the size is stable and predictable
An even split of On-Demand and Spot, regardless of workload shape

scenes.narration: Here's why. Twenty-two minutes clears Lambda's nine-hundred-second ceiling with no exception available — that single fact eliminates it before you weigh anything else. And a workload that's been stable for over a year is exactly the profile Reserved Instances or a Savings Plan are built for: the commitment risk that makes them wrong for something unpredictable simply isn't present here, so the deeper discount is essentially free money.

answers.prompt: A job execution reliably takes twenty-two minutes.
answers.rationale: Lambda's maximum timeout is a hard 900 seconds, 15 minutes — 22 minutes blows past that with no configuration that raises it. EC2, Fargate, and Batch all support long-running executions and are untouched by this fact alone.

answers.prompt: A workload's size has been stable for over a year.
answers.correct: Reserved Instances or a Savings Plan.
answers.rationale: Commitment-based discounts are exactly right once size and duration are already known — that's when you capture the deeper discount with minimal downside. On-Demand's flexibility premium isn't worth paying for a workload that isn't changing, and Spot risks interruption on what's likely an always-on, non-interruption-tolerant workload.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. Lambda's ceiling is nine hundred seconds with no override — check duration first, since it eliminates the most options fastest. Instance family letters are a resource ratio, not a size tier — match the letter to the actual bottleneck. On-Demand, Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, and Spot are three different bets on the same uncertainty, not a ladder from reckless to responsible. Cluster placement groups buy low-latency adjacency at the cost of being confined to one Availability Zone, while spread and partition groups trade that adjacency for fault isolation instead. And the whole E C 2 versus Lambda versus Fargate versus Batch decision comes down to three facts a scenario always hands you: duration, statefulness, and how much control over the host it needs. Next: once you've picked E C 2, what do you actually attach to it — chapter five covers E B S, instance store, and the real storage tradeoffs underneath the compute choice you just made.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: Lambda's ceiling is 900 seconds (15 minutes) with no override — check duration first, it eliminates the most options fastest.
Instance family letters are a resource ratio, not a size tier — match the letter to the bottleneck before you touch the number after it.
On-Demand, Reserved/Savings Plans, and Spot are three different bets on the same uncertainty, not a ranking from reckless to responsible.
Cluster placement groups buy low-latency adjacency at the cost of one Availability Zone; spread and partition trade that for fault isolation.
EC2 vs Lambda vs Fargate vs Batch is answerable from three facts a scenario always gives you: duration, statefulness, and control needed.
